subtype: Approach: using an everyday example to understand fractions [Thinking]
passage: Note from the tutor, Saturday. Sumit stared at three-fourths in his book and said, "It's just two numbers stuck together." His mother came out of the kitchen with a roti, cut it into four equal parts, and put three on his plate. Sumit looked at his plate, and then at the single piece left on the tray. "So the top number is how many I have," he said slowly. "And the bottom is how many parts it was cut into." He drew four boxes in his notebook and shaded three. I said nothing. He explained it to me twice. Chaitanya, tutor

qa.q: How many parts of the roti did Sumit's mother put on his plate?
qa.a: She cut it into four equal parts and put three on his plate.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling before his mother brought the roti, and what changed?
qa.a: He was puzzled and cut off from the idea, since three-fourths seemed like two numbers stuck together. After he saw the food, he became interested and eager to explain.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sumit use to understand other fractions, and why?
qa.a: He could fold a paper into equal parts and shade some. Seeing the parts in something he can hold makes the number less abstract.

qa.q: How might Sumit's mother see what happened at the table?
qa.a: She may feel glad that a small thing from the kitchen made her son understand. She did not explain the number, only cut the roti.

grounding: A boy cannot follow three-fourths until a roti is cut into four parts and he is given three, so real food gives the number a meaning.
